newsitem.title: USA: U.S. nuke industry aims to sell to China by 1998.
newsitem.headline: U.S. nuke industry aims to sell to China by 1998.

text.p: U.S. nuclear power reactor manufacturers, seeing no market at home, are counting on the Clinton administration to clear the way for sales to China by early 1998, an industry official said Thursday.

"We are optimistic that either late this year or early next year commerce with China could begin," said Marvin Fertel, a vice president of the Nuclear Energy Institute, the industry's trade association.
"Our target is the summit this fall," he said, referring to a planned summit between President Bill Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
If an agreement is not signed at the fall summit, then the industry is hoping an accord will be reached by the time the two presidents meet next spring in China.
The U.S. government will not allow sales of nuclear technology to China unless it can certify that Beijing will ensure that the technology does not get into the wrong hands.
The U.S. and Chinese government are "making significant progress in meeting non-proliferation concerns," Fertel said.
However, Beijing's efforts were tarnished last week when the United States slapped sanctions on Chinese companies for transferring chemical weapons components to Iran.

U.S. nuclear technology companies are focusing on China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea as the biggest markets for their advanced new technology, worth billions of dollars, with some potential in Turkey, Hungary and possibly Indonesia.
"There is very little interest anywhere else outside Asia," said Regis Matzie, vice president of nuclear systems engineering for ABB Combustion Engineering Nuclear Power.

Other countries that need new reactors, especially in the Former Soviet Union, do not have the money for them, he said, adding that nuclear energy would have to compete against cheap fossil fuel in eastern Europe and the former Soviet states.

Taiwan Power Co recently awarded General Electric Co's GE Nuclear Energy a $1.8 billion contract for two advanced boiling water reactors, a technology certified last week by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

Unlike the United States, where nuclear power meets about one-fifth of all electricity demand and is likely to slip as markets are deregulated, Japan and South Korea have targeted nuclear energy to supply 40 to 50 percent of their power needs.

For companies like GE and Westinghouse Electric Corp, which is awaiting NRC approval of its new nuclear unit technology, those markets are essential because no utilities are planning to build new nuclear plants in the United States.
